# Finite sample cap crossings and two-sided incidence obstruction

This is a consequence of the explicit signed mass variations in
`candidate 97eab0f821e54041`.
It concerns its strict-compatibility, smooth exposed-patch phase only.
It does not assert that an arbitrary attained minimizer has such patches,
or that the stated crossing condition occurs below the OC target.

## 1. Hypotheses and one common dual for all samples

Retain that note's finite positive actual family, strict compatibility,
maximum depth beta, deepest-base set I, and one arbitrarily selected finite
positive critical circuit at each p in I. All its actual caps H_pj have
positive equal left/right threshold slopes S_pj. Define

    kappa_pj=(rho_pj/S_pj)/sum_l(rho_pl/S_pl)>0,
    A_p(w)=sum_j kappa_pj 1_H_pj(w).

Let Omega consist of measured globally exposed points whose own fiber has
a unique supporting normal and singleton support face. Only points off
all the finitely many selected cap boundaries are used as samples.

For ANY finite sample set W contained in Omega and off these boundaries,
the signed mass theorem implies, at an unrestricted local depth minimum,
the existence of ONE probability vector pi=(pi_p)_(p in I) satisfying

    sum_p pi_p A_p(w)=beta for EVERY w in W.                 (1)

In particular, when W contains sample pairs for many different crossings,
the same pi occurs in every pair's equation. Using different applications
of the theorem for different pairs and silently identifying their dual
weights would be invalid; here all pairs are included at once.

If desired, there is even a common pi for the whole set Omega off the cap
boundaries. For each sample w, its equation (1) defines a closed subset of
the finite-dimensional compact probability simplex. The signed theorem
says every finite intersection is nonempty. Compactness gives a point in
their full intersection. The finite argument below needs no such passage.

## 2. Exact fiber-restricted crossing classes

Fix a base q and an open C1 patch U of boundary K_q, all of whose measured
points belong to Omega. Choose v in U and a continuous affine hyperplane

    L={x: f(x)=u.x-c=0}, |u|=1,

through v, transverse to U there: the restriction of u to the tangent
space T_v U is nonzero. Assume EVERY selected cap whose boundary contains
(q,v) restricts on {q} x R^d to this same unoriented hyperplane L.
This is the isolated-class condition. Other selected cap boundaries have
a nonzero margin at (q,v).

For the crossing class G, write its restrictions as

    H_pj restricted to the q-fiber = {x:s_pj f(x)>=0},
    s_pj in {+1,-1}.                                       (2)

The class must be grouped by restrictions to this measured fiber, not
merely by equality of ambient planes. Different integer normal components
can give the same restricted plane at q. Equal continuous-normal length
one makes (2) exact after the indicated orientation choice.

By transversality, a C1 curve v(t) in U through v has f(v(t)) with strictly
positive derivative at zero, after reversing t if necessary. For small
t>0 set w^+=(q,v(t)) and w^-=(q,v(-t)). These are off every selected cap
boundary. Every cap outside G has the same incidence at both points, by
its strict margin. The caps in G have the incidence differences s_pj.
Consequently

    A_p(w^+)-A_p(w^-)
       =J_p:=sum_(j:(p,j) in G) kappa_pj s_pj.              (3)

This is an exact step difference, not a derivative of an indicator or an
assignment of incidence to the boundary point itself. Closed caps remain
closed, and the sample points carry no ambiguity.

## 3. The finite jump-matrix theorem

Choose finitely many crossings satisfying Section 2, possibly on different
fiber patches. Let J_pc be the jump (3) for base p and crossing c. Choose
their pairs small enough to remain in the stated patches, and put ALL
their points in a single finite set W.

**Theorem.** At an unrestricted local depth minimum under the hypotheses
above there is a probability vector pi on I with

    sum_p pi_p J_pc=0 for EVERY crossing c.                 (4)

Proof. Apply (1) once to this W and subtract the two equations belonging
to each crossing pair. This gives (4) with the same pi throughout.

Thus zero must lie in the convex hull of the row vectors
(J_pc)_c. Equivalently there is no real vector lambda=(lambda_c) for which

    sum_c J_pc lambda_c>0 for EVERY p in I.                 (5)

Indeed (4) rules out (5) by averaging. Conversely, if zero is outside the
finite compact convex hull of the rows, strict separation supplies such a
lambda, with its sign chosen to make all pairings positive. Equation (5)
is therefore an exact finite certificate against local minimality in this
phase. No maximizing center needs to be differentiated.

### 3.1 Unidirectional isolated crossings

Suppose each crossing class can be oriented so that all its caps have
s_pj=+1. Then every J_pc is nonnegative. Equation (4) forces pi_p=0 for
every base p whose selected circuit contributes any cap to that class,
because its contribution kappa_pj is strictly positive.

If the union of these classes includes at least one cap from EVERY deepest
base's selected circuit, all pi_p are zero, contradicting sum_p pi_p=1.
Hence that finite crossing configuration is impossible at a local minimum
under these hypotheses. It suffices in particular that each selected
deepest circuit has one cap admitting its own isolated transverse crossing
on such a patch. At most two sample points per chosen crossing are needed.

A SINGLE uncancelled cap crossing, by itself, only forces zero dual weight
on its owning base. It is a contradiction when there is a unique deepest
base, or when other selected crossing equations eliminate all remaining
bases. Ignoring possible zero dual weights would overstate the result.

### 3.2 Coincident opposite orientations

When G contains both orientations, (4) says precisely

    sum_p pi_p sum_(j in G_p,s_pj=+1) kappa_pj
       =sum_p pi_p sum_(j in G_p,s_pj=-1) kappa_pj.          (6)

There is then no general positivity contradiction. For example two
opposite halfspaces through an ordinary ball center, with circuit weights
1/2 and 1/2, have score identically 1/2 off their common boundary. Their
jumps cancel at every transverse crossing of that plane with the sphere.
This is an actual smooth case, showing why opposite orientations cannot
be discarded.

Several distinct restricted planes can also pass through a single patch
point. That point does not satisfy the isolated-class hypothesis. If a
specific pair of nearby samples can instead be found, one may use its
ACTUAL finite incidence difference in (3)--(5); there is no automatic
single-plane jump formula at such an intersection.

## 4. Scope relative to existing variational conditions

The new finite obstruction uses the realized signed local masses to keep
one dual probability vector for sample pairs on both sides of multiple
cap crossings. It adds exact cancellation equations on restricted cap
planes to the inward-only incidence inequalities. The archive already
contains aggregate stationarity and smooth signed boundary variations;
those facts alone do not justify changing the dual weights independently
from one crossing to the next.

The required two-sided geometric feasibility is essential. Ordinary
polytope vertices fail the smooth singleton-normal hypothesis. Active
compatibility can send outward hull mass to other fibers even when every
own fiber is a Euclidean ball, as the exact ball-cylinder example in the
preceding note proves. Nor do the present arguments guarantee all selected
caps admit isolated transverse crossings on feasible patches. Consequently
this theorem is a local obstruction under explicit conditions, not an
arbitrary-body classification or a resolution of (OC).
